task_row_model.query: In adult outpatients diagnosed with uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia, what are the recommended first-line antibiotic options, typical dosages, and the suggested duration of therapy?

documents.content: Pediatric guidelines for community-acquired pneumonia emphasize different pathogens and dosing compared with adults. In children, high-dose amoxicillin is used to cover Streptococcus pneumoniae, with weight-based dosing and narrower age-specific recommendations. Viral causes are common in younger children, so supportive care and watchful waiting are often appropriate for mild cases. Decisions about antibiotics incorporate immunization status and age-specific risk factors. While some antibiotic classes overlap with adult therapy, dosing frequency, formulations and thresholds for hospitalization differ substantially between pediatric and adult practice, limiting direct applicability of pediatric recommendations to adult outpatients.

Uncomplicated urinary tract infection (UTI) management in nonpregnant adults typically involves nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for five days or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for three days when local resistance is low. Fluoroquinolones are generally avoided as first-line for uncomplicated cystitis due to collateral damage and resistance concerns. For pyelonephritis, longer durations and broader-spectrum oral agents or initial intravenous therapy may be required depending on severity and comorbidities. Urine culture guidance and local antibiogram data are important for choosing empiric therapy and adjusting treatment after results.

For adult outpatients with uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia who are otherwise healthy, recommended first-line options include high-dose amoxicillin (commonly 1 g orally three times daily) to cover Streptococcus pneumoniae. Alternatives are doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily or a macrolide such as azithromycin (500 mg on day 1, then 250 mg daily on days 2–5) when local pneumococcal resistance to macrolides is low. For patients with comorbidities, a beta-lactam plus macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone are options. The usual duration for uncomplicated outpatient therapy is minimum five days, and treatment can be stopped after at least five days if the patient is clinically stable and afebrile for 48–72 hours.

Asthma management centers on controller and reliever therapy. Inhaled corticosteroids are the mainstay for persistent asthma to reduce airway inflammation, with dosing adjusted by severity. Short-acting beta-agonists are used for acute symptom relief. Long-acting beta-agonists are combined with inhaled corticosteroids for moderate to severe disease. Education on inhaler technique, trigger avoidance, and an individualized action plan are essential. For severe exacerbations, systemic corticosteroids and adjunctive oxygen or bronchodilator therapy may be necessary. These strategies differ from antibiotic decision-making for infectious respiratory conditions.

In hospitalized or severe cases of community-acquired pneumonia, empiric therapy often involves intravenous beta-lactams and broader-spectrum agents due to risk of resistant organisms or atypical pathogens. Treatment durations in inpatient settings commonly extend to seven to ten days, depending on clinical response and stability. Switching from IV to oral therapy occurs once the patient is improving and can tolerate oral intake. Decisions about agent selection and exact duration rely on severity scores, comorbidities, and microbiology results; this inpatient-focused guidance only partially applies to otherwise healthy outpatients with uncomplicated disease.
